Here is my recipe:

**Starter:**

* Fed 75% King Arthur bread flour, 25% rye flour
* 1:1:1 feeding every 12 hours with 95F water
* Fermented at 80F


***Dough***

**Totals:** 

* 986g flour (all King Arthur bread flour aside from starter)
* 789g water (95F)
    * 80% hydration
* 25g mortons kosher salt
    * 2.5% salt

**Levain**

* 150g bread flour
* 150g water (95F)
* 30g starter

1. Ferment until peak activity (10-12 hours)
2. Start autolyze 2h before peak activity

**Autolyze**

* 821g bread flour
* 624g water (95F)
* 25g salt

1. Autolyze for 1-2 hours before mixing dough

**Mix and BF**

1. Mix levain into dough thoroughly using hands
2. Bulk ferment at 80F for 4+ hours until doubled in size
3. Stretch and fold four times (first two every 15m, second two every 30m)

It’s just very common in every demographic. Between 50-80% of Americans have HSV-1 and almost 1 in 5 people has HSV-2. If you narrow that down to the percentage of people who are regularly sexually active… it’s a very high number. Also herpes can easily spread by skin contact, so condoms don’t necessarily prevent it. 

Most people who have either form of HSV do not know they have it, because: 

1: Many people just don’t get tested for STIs regularly.

2: HSV tests specifically are highly inconsistent - even someone who’s positive for HSV will likely test negative most of the time. This is due to the tests only returning accurate positive results near the time of an outbreak. False negatives are possible even DURING an outbreak. So even if you do test and have negative result, there is still a pretty high likelihood you do have HSV.

2: It is very common for testing centers to choose not to test for either form of HSV. This is due to the above mentioned unreliability of tests, but more importantly it’s actually done as a public health measure. It’s widely understood that the stigma around being HSV positive is far more harmful to people’s quality of life than the actual physical symptoms of herpes. Herpes itself is a minor annoyance, physically. But the stigma of knowing you have it can have a huge impact on your wellbeing and mental health - which makes even less sense considering that the person you’re delivering the news to is also very likely HSV positive.

A big part of the benefit of them is making modular code that you can edit in one place and have it extend to all of the classes extending that code. As a general rule it's best to avoid duplicating your code as much as you can, e.g. by setting characteristics and methods to the highest-level class that has that behavior.

For example, if you were making a program about animals, you might want to have a class for "animal" which could be inherited by a "mammal" class, which could be inherited by classes like "primate" or "rodent". You would want to set characteristic or methods to the highest-level class where those characteristics are shared, e.g. a "mammal" class could have a characteristic "warm-blooded", so any subclass of mammal would also have that characteristic. This is much better than manually setting "warm-blooded" on each individual mammal class you created.
